title: The light has left the body, not vanished
question: Does the combined isolated system lose energy when the body emits?
recap: The body’s loss is the radiation’s gain; distinguish a calculation, a broader inference, and an experimental test.
premises: The larger account includes the body and all the light it emitted.
No energy crosses that larger boundary.
limitations: A successful model calculation is not an observed experimental confirmation.
The 1906 box argument and modern four-momentum are separate extensions.

overview.text: Draw a larger boundary around the body and its light. What left the body remains inside that larger system. The result calls for a test; the calculation itself does not supply one.

full.text: An account of the body alone loses the emitted energy. An account including the body and both pulses retains its total energy in each frame. Losing energy from one subsystem does not mean energy has disappeared from the isolated whole.

The paper closes by proposing systems with strongly varying energy content, such as radium salts, as possible tests, and leaves the physical claim conditional on agreement with facts. This preview supplies neither a new experiment nor a transcription of those sentences.

The system-boundaries laboratory lets you distinguish the body, radiation, and combined-system boundaries. Its modern invariant-mass interpretation and dated 1906 box extension are additional explanations, not steps secretly inserted into the 1905 inference.

items: Choose a boundary before reading any change of energy. The same emission reads differently depending on what the boundary encloses.
Body only: energy L has crossed the boundary outward, in the rest frame, and the body’s account records a loss.
Radiation only: the two departing pulses carry the emitted energy, L in total in the rest frame, and this account records a gain.
Body and all of the light together: nothing has crossed the larger boundary, so its total energy is the same before and after, in each frame separately.
A loss from one subsystem is therefore not a disappearance from the isolated whole. The light has left the body; it has not vanished.

The paper proposes bodies whose energy content varies strongly, such as radium salts, as possible tests, and leaves the physical claim conditional on agreement with facts. A prediction is not an observation: keep the conditional prediction apart from any independently calibrated measurement.

Return to the chain of the argument and name its three ingredients: the imported transformation of light energy, the premise that the offset between the two accounts does not change, and the low-speed identification that turns the kinetic-energy drop into a mass difference.
The system-boundaries laboratory lets you move the boundary yourself. Its modern invariant-mass reading and the 1906 box extension are later explanations, not steps hidden inside the 1905 inference.

margin.text: Two oppositely directed light pulses can have nonzero invariant mass as a combined system even though individual photons have zero rest mass. That statement uses modern energy–momentum accounting; it is not a premise of the 1905 two-ledger route.
